rejected_explanations:
Seven explanations were considered and REJECTED, each with the number that rejected it.

1. 'PostgreSQL wins because it parallelises and CUBRID does not.' REJECTED. F_units = 1.029635x. CUBRID's trace reports parallel workers: 5 on the driving scan; PostgreSQL reports Workers Launched: 4 plus a participating leader. Measured units: CUBRID U 4.25201 / TWU 4.2459 / peak 5.3223; PostgreSQL U 4.37802 / TWU 4.4629 / peak 4.7943. perf stat independently reports 4.285 vs 4.436 CPUs utilized. A controlled serialisation of CUBRID measures U 1.00238 and reproduces the resulting wall ratio to 0.057%. The units term explains 2.96% of a 124.6% gap.

2. 'CUBRID re-reads pages PostgreSQL keeps resident (IMP-002/IMP-010/IMP-018).' REJECTED twice over. /proc/<server>/io read_bytes is 0 for BOTH engines, Num_data_page_ioreads delta 0, pg_stat_database.blks_read delta 0, and the serial-vs-parallel probe puts CUBRID's page fixes within 0.00067% of each other (22,649,042 vs 22,648,891). There is no I/O term in this query at all.

3. 'CUBRID does more work -- more rows, more page fixes.' REJECTED. Ground truth G0-G8 is identical on both engines including the 15,337,604-row join output, and matched-node page fixes agree to 1.000259x. Whole-statement page fixes do differ more (22,649,042 vs 19,505,873 = 1.161140x) and that 1.16x is honestly part of the story, but it cannot produce a 2.198x CPU ratio on its own, and the CPU is concentrated in a band that runs the same 15,000,000 times on both engines.

4. 'It is the 15.3M-row temp materialisation and sort.' REJECTED as the DOMINANT cause, retained as a real ~16% contributor. The trace puts the inner GROUP BY at 2,202 ms of 13,357 ms; the profile puts CUBRID's whole aggregation band at 5.12% = 2.481 core-s of 48.4559. Both readings say the same thing: a sixth of the problem, not the problem. It is given its own controlled A/B rather than folded into a factor.

5. 'CUBRID is memory-stalled / cache-hostile on this access pattern.' REJECTED, and the counter runs the OTHER way: CUBRID's IPC is 1.73 against PostgreSQL's 1.19. CUBRID's pipelines are better fed; it simply issues 3.1220x the instructions.

6. 'The LIKE gap is a collation/charset artifact.' REJECTED, and checked BEFORE the band was interpreted. tpch_sspq is encoding UTF8, so like.c:156-161 routes to UTF8_MatchText, not the SB_MatchText single-byte path; CUBRID's column is COLLATE utf8_bin under intl_collation=utf8_bin. Both engines run a UTF-8, deterministic, binary-ordering LIKE over the same bytes.

7. 'PostgreSQL's plan is simply better, so CUBRID's executor is fine.' REJECTED. When PostgreSQL is denied its ordered parallel path it takes 13.678 s, i.e. CUBRID is 1.1972x FASTER than PostgreSQL on the shape CUBRID is confined to. The plan is worth a lot, but the executor gap is real, separable, and where 46-48% of the CPU difference lives.

source_contrast:
Eight rows with file:line on BOTH sides.

(1) PER-CHARACTER UTF-8 LIKE COMPARISON. CUBRID src/base/language_support.c:2852-2908 -- the match loop calls intl_utf8_to_cp() on BOTH operands (:2857, :2858) to build codepoints, then maps each through the collation weight table weight_ptr[cp1]/weight_ptr[cp2] (:2877, :2893) before comparing (:2901). utf8_bin is a BINARY collation whose weight for every codepoint is the codepoint itself, yet the loop still pays two decodes and two table lookups per character; there is no memcmp/byte-lockstep path and no ASCII fast path in the function. PostgreSQL src/backend/utils/adt/like.c:128-134 -- for UTF-8 it compiles a DEDICATED specialization: '#define NextChar(p, plen) do { (p)++; (plen)--; } while ((plen) > 0 && (*(p) & 0xC0) == 0x80)' with '#define MatchText UTF8_MatchText', i.e. character advance is a pointer increment plus a continuation-byte test on raw bytes -- no decode, no table, no call. The general multibyte path it deliberately avoids is at :96-98 (pg_mblen_with_len, wchareq). CLASS: STRUCTURAL ABSENCE.

(2) CANDIDATE-POSITION SEARCH FOR %pattern%. CUBRID language_support.c:2831-2908 is re-entered per candidate start position from qstr_eval_like; every candidate position pays the full decode+weight loop from its first character. PostgreSQL src/backend/utils/adt/like_match.c:174-185 -- the % scan tests GETCHAR(*t) == firstpat, ONE BYTE COMPARE per text byte, and only recurses into MatchText on a byte hit; :366-372 further documents using NextByte rather than NextChar mid-match because 'we must already have matched at least one byte of the character'. CLASS: STRUCTURAL ABSENCE.

(3) ADMITTING AN INDEX SCAN WHOSE ONLY VALUE IS ORDERING. CUBRID src/optimizer/query_planner.c:9239-9246 -- a QO_SCANMETHOD_INDEX_GROUPBY_SCAN plan IS generated when the node has no sargable terms but the query has a GROUP BY and qo_validate_index_for_groupby() passes. It is handed straight to qo_check_plan_on_info(), which at :6014-6019 releases it if plan->plan_un.scan.index->head->groupby_skip is false. That flag is written ONLY at :1172-1175, inside qo_top_plan_new(), and ONLY when the final top plan is itself QO_PLANTYPE_SCAN. So whenever the query contains a join the flag is still false at admission time, the plan is released at birth, and qo_generate_seq_scan() at :9283 supplies the only surviving access path. PostgreSQL src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c:965-966 -- 'if (index_clauses != NIL || useful_pathkeys != NIL || useful_predicate || index_only_scan)' creates the index path BECAUSE the ordering is useful, with no restriction to single-relation queries, and :984-1003 creates the parallel variant with the same useful_pathkeys. CLASS: STRUCTURAL ABSENCE.

(4) THE SAME OPTIMIZATION'S OWN ORDER BY TWIN, INSIDE CUBRID. query_planner.c:6006-6012 -- the ORDER BY arm of the SAME FUNCTION reads '!(plan->top_rooted ? plan->plan_un.scan.index->head->orderby_skip : qo_plan_is_orderby_skip_candidate (plan))', i.e. it HAS a pre-top-rooted candidate predicate (:12559-12610, which computes the sort list on the spot via qo_plan_compute_iscan_sort_list() at :12603). The GROUP BY arm at :6015 has no such branch. This is an asymmetry WITHIN CUBRID: the fix already exists six lines above the defect. CLASS: SAME STAGE, LOWER MEASURED COST.

(5) PROPAGATING AN INDEX ORDER THROUGH A JOIN. CUBRID query_planner.c:12271-12291 -- qo_plan_compute_iscan_sort_list() DOES walk down a join ('case QO_PLANTYPE_JOIN: plan = plan->plan_un.join.outer;'), so CUBRID is architecturally able to read an ordering off a join's outer side; :12310 then requires that leaf to satisfy qo_is_interesting_order_scan(). In Q13 the leaf is sscan customer, because item (3) already deleted the index alternative. PostgreSQL src/backend/optimizer/path/pathkeys.c:1294-1318 -- build_join_pathkeys() returns the outer path's pathkeys unchanged for every join type EXCEPT JOIN_FULL/JOIN_RIGHT/JOIN_RIGHT_ANTI (:1303-1306); Q13's join is LEFT so the order survives, and src/backend/optimizer/util/pathnode.c:2420 stores it on the NestPath. CLASS: COMMON TO BOTH ENGINES -- both can carry an order through a nested loop; only PostgreSQL still has an ordered path to carry.

(6) CONSUMING A PRE-EXISTING ORDER IN THE GROUPING NODE. CUBRID src/query/query_executor.c:16605-16609 -- the sort-free grouping routine qexec_groupby_index() is reachable only when xasl->spec_list->indexptr->groupby_skip is set, i.e. only when THIS XASL's own first access spec is an index scan carrying the flag; a join's XASL cannot satisfy that. query_planner.c:1192 is the consequence: 'plan = qo_sort_new (plan, QO_UNORDERED, SORT_GROUPBY)', an unconditional sort. PostgreSQL src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c:7959-8003 -- make_ordered_path() returns the path UNCHANGED when pathkeys_count_contained_in() says it is already sorted, inserting no Sort node at all; :7436-7446 then builds create_agg_path(..., AGG_SORTED, ...) on top. CLASS: STRUCTURAL ABSENCE.

(7) BUFFER FIX / PIN COST PER PAGE. CUBRID src/storage/page_buffer.c pgbuf_fix_release 13.86% self, pgbuf_unfix 3.49%, pgbuf_replace_watcher 1.07% plus 2.31 points of libpthread mutex traffic underneath them, 10.210 core-s per statement. PostgreSQL src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c PinBuffer 7.74%, StartReadBuffer 1.13%, UnpinBufferNoOwner 0.87% plus hash_search_with_hash_value 10.19% and LWLockAttemptLock 6.69%, 7.006 core-s. For an EQUAL number of page fixes at the matched node (19,504,609 vs 19,499,552 = 1.000259x) CUBRID spends 1.4573x the CPU. CLASS: SAME STAGE, LOWER MEASURED COST.

(8) ROW MATERIALISATION. CUBRID src/storage/heap_file.c heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues 2.89%, heap_prepare_get_context 1.01%, heap_init_get_context 0.68%; src/storage/slotted_page.c spage_get_record 4.00%; src/object/object_representation.c or_mvcc_get_repid_and_flags 2.48%, or_header_size 0.31%; src/object/object_primitive.c pr_clear_value 0.77%; mr_readval_string_internal 1.51% -- 8.315 core-s per statement building and tearing down typed DB_VALUEs. PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/execTuples.c tts_buffer_heap_getsomeattrs 1.74% deforms into a flat Datum/isnull array with cached attribute offsets and NO per-value teardown; the rest of PostgreSQL's 4.895 core-s band is heap_page_prune_opt 12.77% and heap_hot_search_buffer 6.75%, which are MVCC maintenance CUBRID does elsewhere -- so the 1.6987x is reported WITH that caveat and no exact-equivalence claim. CLASS: SAME STAGE, LOWER MEASURED COST.

SEARCHES PERFORMED FOR CLAIMS OF ABSENCE (SSOT section 17): grep -rn over src/base/language_support.c, src/base/intl_support.c and src/query/string_opfunc.c for 'memcmp', 'bin', 'fast', 'ascii', 'lockstep', 'byte' around lang_strmatch_utf8/qstr_eval_like -- NO byte-lockstep or binary-collation fast path exists; the only branch on collation type inside the matcher is 'lang_coll->built_in && ignore_trailing_space' at :2843, which selects a different WEIGHT TABLE, not a different algorithm. For item (3), groupby_skip was traced through all 20 of its occurrences in src/optimizer/ and src/parser/ (query_planner.c, plan_generation.c, query_graph.c/.h, xasl_generation.c); the flag is written in exactly ONE place, query_planner.c:1174.

buffer_state_of_the_headline: Q14 is NOT a zero-physical-read query on either engine, unlike Q13. The working set exceeds both engines' equal 8192 MB budget (CUBRID lineitem 10,670.9 MiB + part 380.5 MiB; PostgreSQL 8,790 MB + 320 MB). Per measured statement, from /proc/<pid>/io sampled across EVERY engine PID: CUBRID 431,446 read syscalls moving 7.068 GB -- exactly 16,383 B per call, one 16 KiB page per miss, a 63.2% miss rate against lineitem's 682,937 heap pages -- against PostgreSQL's 49,077-84,844 syscalls for 1.19-1.87 GB (pg_statio 119,543 blks_read/statement of 1,166,112 = 10.3%). DEVICE reads are ZERO on both sides, so this is not disk latency: it is CPU spent copying pages the engine already read, visible as CUBRID's 2.940 core-s/statement copy band. PostgreSQL additionally writes ~258 MB/statement of hash-spill temp. WARM is therefore satisfied in the SSOT s12 sense (proved-stationary, three block medians within 0.69%/0.79%) but Q14's WARM is STATIONARY-WITH-MISSES, not Q13's stronger proved-stationary-and-zero-miss. That distinction is stated, not glossed.
carried_forward_gaps: 1. Q14's F_cost residual (1.679358x) is attributed by profile bands, not by a controlled A/B -- the same evidence class as Q12/Q13's F_cost. 2. The list-file materialisation of CUBRID's hash-join inputs (section 8-d) is identified with a mechanism but not quantified, because no controlled A/B isolates it on Q14. 3. IMP-011's proposed per-page spill charge is validated in DIRECTION and MAGNITUDE on Q14 but not implemented, so its status stays 'measured', not 'validated'. 4. The stage-14.7 CUBRID statdump band is unavailable on this server (see above); the /proc-based substitute is whole-process and cannot be split per plan node.
causal_decomposition_narrative:
F_PLAN REPRODUCED ARITHMETICALLY FROM THREE SOURCE CONSTANTS.
qo_hjoin_cost() computes, for the outer-as-build order:
  outer_build_cpu = inner_card x QO_CPU_WEIGHT x HJ_PROBE_CPU_OVERHEAD_FACTOR
                  + outer_card x QO_CPU_WEIGHT x HJ_BUILD_CPU_OVERHEAD_FACTOR
                  + HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT
                  = 2,000,000 x 0.0025 x 20 + 752,032 x 0.0025 x 40 + 1,500
                  = 100,000 + 75,203.2 + 1,500 = 176,703.2
  832,902 (lineitem sscan) + 29,353 (part sscan) + 176,703.2 + 1,469 (outer_pages)
    = 1,040,427  <- EXACTLY the cost CUBRID prints at max_hash_list_scan_size=128M
  spill = (2,000,000 + 752,032) x 0.5 = 1,376,016
  1,040,427 + 1,376,016 = 2,416,443  <- EXACTLY the cost CUBRID prints at 8 MB
The reconstruction is exact to the unit, so the ENTIRE difference between the two hash-join costs is the spill penalty.
  idx-join cost (chosen)           1,220,202
  hash-join cost at 8 MB (rejected) 2,416,443
  decision margin                  1,196,241
  spill penalty                    1,376,016 = 115% of the margin
  HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT                1,500 = 0.13% of the margin
Removing the spill term alone flips the choice -- not a hypothesis: setting max_hash_list_scan_size=128M removes it and CUBRID picks the hash join with NO hint.

HOW WRONG IS THE PENALTY? Anchoring the cost scale on the native plan (1,220,202 units <-> 3.228 s => 2.6455 us/unit), 1,376,016 units implies 3.640 s of wall. Measured SPLIT time: 0.089 s of a 3,244 ms statement. OVERCHARGED 40.9x. A per-page charge -- inner_pages + outer_pages ~ 4,521 units -- would have let the hash plan win on cost.

EXPLANATIONS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, each with the number that rejected it:
 * 'The hash memory budget is too small.' REJECTED BY 79 ms. 16x more memory does not help: 128 MB single-batch 2.959 s vs 8 MB partitioned 2.880 s -- the bigger budget is 0.0274x SLOWER. Also disposes of 'scale max_hash_list_scan_size with data_buffer_size' as Q14's fix.
 * 'CUBRID is bad at parallelism.' REJECTED: CUBRID 5.5802x speedup at +7.0% CPU (93.6% efficiency vs U) against PostgreSQL 3.8837x at +39.1% (67.2%). F_units 1.001341x is INSIDE the 0.7869% error budget.
 * 'HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT causes it.' REJECTED: 0.13% of the margin (Q09 rejected it at 0.16% for the same reason).
 * 'CUBRID scans more rows.' REJECTED by ground truth: exactly 59,986,052 both engines, confirmed by each engine's own count(*), CUBRID's six-worker trace sum, and PostgreSQL's Rows Removed by Filter + output rows.
 * 'The dialect interval translation penalises CUBRID.' REJECTED BY DIRECTION: it forces a date->timestamp promotion on PostgreSQL, the WINNER, so it is conservative. Row sets proved identical (749,223 both forms, pg_typeof = timestamp without time zone).
 * 'It is physical I/O.' REJECTED as DISK I/O: device reads 0 MiB on both engines. It is real but it is CPU spent copying page-cache pages (2.940 vs 1.254 core-s per statement) and is counted inside F_cost.

WHAT REMAINS: fixing F_plan alone moves R_wall from 1.884804x to 1.681625x. The residual is F_cost 1.679358x on F_work exactly 1.0 -- 277.17 vs 165.04 ns per row.

A STRUCTURAL COST CUBRID'S HASH JOIN STILL PAYS: even when it runs the hash join, the trace shows both inputs first materialised into temp list files (SUBQUERY (uncorrelated) feeding SCAN (temp ...) of 749,223 rows) where PostgreSQL streams the probe side straight through Parallel Hash Join. This is why CUBRID's forced hash join reaches 2.880 s and not PostgreSQL's 1.713 s. Relates to IMP-006; recorded as an observation, not quantified, because no controlled A/B isolates it.
causal_multiplier_summary:
R_wall 1.884804x [wall, median of 3 per engine, contract block1; PostgreSQL faster] = F_plan 1.120833x [plan-shape; same-engine CUBRID A/B] x F_units 1.001341x [total-query-CPU/wall correction, cross-checked by TWU] x F_cpu 1.679358x [total query CPU-seconds]. headline_finding:
Q14 is the first query in this campaign with a NUMERIC F_plan, and its plan half reduces to ONE per-row constant in the CUBRID cost model.

The two engines choose structurally different plans. CUBRID picks a nested-loop idx-join: scan lineitem with the shipdate sarg, then probe part's primary-key B-tree 749,222 times at EXACTLY 4.0000 page fetches per probe (2,996,858 fetches total). PostgreSQL picks a 32-batch Parallel Hash Join over all of part. Both nonetheless scan exactly the same 59,986,052 lineitem rows, so F_work is exactly 1.000000 and the plan effect is isolated cleanly.

THE PLAN HALF IS ONE CONSTANT. CUBRID costs its idx-join 1,220,202 and the hash join over the SAME two scans 2,416,443. The difference is exactly (2,000,000 + 752,032) x HJ_FILE_IO_WEIGHT 0.5 = 1,376,016 -- 115% of the 1,196,241 decision margin. The 1,040,427 base is reproduced to the unit from three source constants (QO_CPU_WEIGHT 0.0025, HJ_BUILD_CPU_OVERHEAD_FACTOR 40, HJ_PROBE_CPU_OVERHEAD_FACTOR 20) plus the two scan costs. Forced onto the hash shape at the SAME default 8 MB budget, CUBRID measures 2.880 s against 3.228 s native: the cost model rates the winner 1.98x MORE EXPENSIVE than the loser. That is a ranking inversion, not a magnitude error.

THE SPILL IS REAL AND NEARLY FREE. The 8 MB hash run genuinely partitions -- the trace prints 'SPLIT (time: 89, partitions: 6)' and 'BUILD ... method: hybrid', against 'BUILD ... method: memory' with no SPLIT node at 128 MB. The partition count is predicted EXACTLY by the in-tree formula: ceil(749,223 x 52 B / (8 MiB x 0.8)) = 6, which independently confirms both the 52-byte per-entry size and the threshold arithmetic. The measured cost of that spill is 89 ms of a 3,244 ms statement (2.7%), while the cost model charges 1,376,016 units -- implying 3.640 s on the native plan's own cost scale. OVERCHARGED BY 40.9x.

WHAT Q14 IS NOT, each rejected with the number that rejected it. NOT the memory budget: the 128 MB single-batch run (2.959 s) is 0.0274x SLOWER than the 8 MB partitioned run (2.880 s), so 'give the hash join more memory' is rejected by 79 ms and the defect is the VALUATION of spilling, not the amount of memory. NOT parallelism: CUBRID's own NO_PARALLEL_SCAN A/B gives 5.5802x speedup for a 7.0% CPU surcharge (93.6% efficiency) against PostgreSQL's 3.8837x for 39.1% (67.2%) -- CUBRID's parallel scan is the BETTER implementation here and F_units is 1.001341x. NOT HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT, the explicit anti-hash offset: 1,500 is 0.13% of the margin. NOT the dialect: the PostgreSQL translation forces a date->timestamp promotion on the engine that WINS, so it is conservative, and the two forms select the identical 749,223 rows. NOT disk I/O: device reads are 0 MiB on both engines.

AND FROM THE OTHER SIDE: PostgreSQL forced onto CUBRID's nested-loop-index shape measures 2.086580 s against 1.712645 s native, so the hash shape is worth 1.2183x to PostgreSQL and 1.1208x to CUBRID on the same data. Both cost models are asked the same question; only CUBRID's answers wrong.

WHAT REMAINS after the plan is fixed: R_wall would move from 1.884804x to 1.681625x, and the residual is a pure CPU-per-row difference of 277.17 ns vs 165.04 ns over identical rows -- largest identified component per-row tuple materialisation at 8.514 vs 5.946 core-s per statement (1.4318x).

source_contrast:
Every row is a concrete file:line on BOTH sides.

1. HASH-JOIN SPILL ACCOUNTING DECIDES PLAN CHOICE [same stage, lower measured cost]
   CUBRID src/optimizer/query_planner.c:3650-3658 -- 'inner_build_io_cost += (inner_cardinality + outer_cardinality) * HJ_FILE_IO_WEIGHT' once the build exceeds max_hash_list_scan_size * HJ_PARTITION_FILL_FACTOR; query_planner.c:90 '#define HJ_FILE_IO_WEIGHT 0.5' -- PER ROW.
   PostgreSQL src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c:4386-4423 initial_cost_hashjoin() -- calls ExecChooseHashTableSize(), and when numbatches > 1 charges seq_page_cost * (inner_pages + outer_pages), i.e. PER PAGE for the predicted batches, and NEVER disqualifies the path.
   Difference: CUBRID bills 1,376,016 units for a spill that measures 89 ms.

2. ANTI-HASH HEURISTIC OFFSET [structural absence]
   CUBRID src/optimizer/query_planner.c:87 -- '#define HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT 1500 /* Heuristic offset to prefer NL join over hash join */'.
   PostgreSQL: no counterpart. Searched the hash-join cost path (initial_cost_hashjoin/final_cost_hashjoin in costsize.c); no constant exists whose stated purpose is to prefer one join method. Named for completeness only -- 0.13% of Q14's margin, NOT a deciding term.

3. HASH MEMORY BUDGET AND HOW IT SCALES [same stage, lower measured cost]
   CUBRID src/base/system_parameter.c:3519-3532 -- max_hash_list_scan_size, default 8 MB, hard maximum 128 MB, a flat per-statement budget that does not scale with data_buffer_size or with parallelism.
   PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/nodeHash.c:3680-3691 get_hash_memory_limit() = work_mem * hash_mem_multiplier; nodeHash.c:717-734 -- Parallel Hash multiplies it by (parallel_workers + 1) to use the COMBINED budget, falling back to per-worker batching rather than avoiding the plan. PostgreSQL gets 8 MB x 6 = 48 MB and still batches to 32 when that is not enough.
   MEASURED NOT TO BE Q14'S DECIDING TERM (rejected by 79 ms) -- recorded because it is the structural difference a reader will expect to be the cause.

4. SPILL THRESHOLD ARITHMETIC, COST MODEL vs EXECUTOR [common to both engines]
   CUBRID src/optimizer/query_planner.c:94 HJ_HASH_ENTRY_POS_SIZE 12 and :91 HJ_PARTITION_FILL_FACTOR 0.8, mirroring src/query/query_hash_join.c:1356 'part_cnt = CEIL_PTVDIV(per_entry_size * min_tuple_cnt, mem_limit * PARTITION_FILL_FACTOR)' with per_entry_size = 2*sizeof(MHT_HLS_SLOT) + sizeof(MHT_HLS_ENTRY) + sizeof(QFILE_TUPLE_SIMPLE_POS) = 52 B.
   PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/nodeHash.c:683-760 ExecChooseHashTableSize() returns nbatch and the planner costs that same nbatch.
   The two CUBRID sites agree with each other AND with the trace (6 partitions predicted, 6 observed). The defect is the PRICE, not the THRESHOLD.

5. PER-ROW TUPLE MATERIALISATION -- the F_cost residual [same stage, lower measured cost]
   CUBRID heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues 9.64%, or_mvcc_get_header 2.22%, spage_get_record 2.52%, pr_clear_value 1.25% -- a fully-typed DB_VALUE built and torn down per attribute per row.
   PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/execTuples.c tts_buffer_heap_getsomeattrs -> slot_deform_heap_tuple 36.73% -- deform into a flat Datum/isnull array using cached attribute offsets, no per-value type object and no teardown.
   8.514 vs 5.946 core-s per statement on identical 59,986,052 rows.

6. SCAN PREDICATE EVALUATION [same stage, lower measured cost]
   CUBRID eval_pred 8.94% + tp_value_compare_with_error 3.66% + eval_value_rel_cmp 3.03% -- generic DB_VALUE comparator with per-call domain resolution.

causal_decomposition_narrative:
WHERE THE 11 SECONDS GO. Both engines spend the session on two sequential expansions of revenue0; only the unit count per expansion differs. CUBRID: 5560 ms @ 6 workers + 5528 ms @ 6 workers + ~33 ms lookup/order = 11121 ms. PostgreSQL: 2340 ms @ 6 units (5 workers + participating leader) + 8817 ms @ ONE unit + ~18 ms = 11235 ms. PostgreSQL executes one expansion 2.38x FASTER than CUBRID executes one, and the other 1.59x SLOWER. The two errors nearly cancel — that is the entire reason Q15 lands at 0.9794x instead of somewhere far from 1.

WHY THE SECOND SUBTREE GETS NOTHING. An InitPlan is evaluated LAZILY, at first reference to its PARAM_EXEC (nodeSubplan.c:1094-1118 ExecSetParamPlan, reached from ExecEvalParamExec). Q15's reference is the outer Finalize GroupAggregate's Filter, so by the time it fires the sibling Gather Merge has already registered 5 parallel workers, and bgworker.c:1103-1112 refuses every further parallel worker once parallel_register_count - parallel_terminate_count >= max_parallel_workers (=5). CUBRID's equivalent pool is sized from PRM_ID_MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS = 100 (px_worker_manager_global.cpp:57,77-78) and try_reserve_workers() (:97-138) even grants PARTIAL reservations, so its second 6-worker expansion draws from 94 free slots.

CONTROLS, all through the same load gate and the same block regime: PostgreSQL native 10.664912 s; PostgreSQL serial (max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0) 16.789883 s, so the gather buys only 1.5743x — far less than 6x, precisely because only ONE expansion ever gets workers; PostgreSQL with the GLOBAL pool at 12 and the per-gather cap still 5: 4.484525 s, with the plan PROVING both subtrees now launch 5 (InitPlan Workers Launched: 5 AND sibling Workers Launched: 5, Execution Time 4571.757 ms) = 2.3782x faster than native and 2.3291x faster than CUBRID. That control is explicitly OUTSIDE the s9 contract and never a headline value; it exists so the report can separate 'PostgreSQL serialises an InitPlan' (FALSE) from 'the configured global pool of 5 was already fully consumed' (TRUE, and measured).

WHAT CUBRID'S SERIAL GROUP-BY COSTS. sort_check_parallelism() returns 1 whenever hash_eligible is set (external_sort.c:5229-5234), and xasl_generation.c:16555-16571 sets that flag PURELY SYNTACTICALLY — a hint or an aggregate-type tree walk, with no cost comparison against the parallel sort group-by it disables. /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ clears it and the trace changes exactly as the source predicts: 'hash: false, sort: true' PLUS '(parallel workers: 3, time: 330..338)', GROUPBY 2644/2636 -> 2305/2220 ms, statement total 11121 -> 10305 ms. The whole-session effect is recorded as a BOUND, not a direct A/B, because the variant's gated block was REJECTED by the s12 WARM gate on ALL FOUR attempts (trailing spread 3.94%, 5.37%, 6.16%, 5.68%, all above the 3.00% sanity bound): across 80 uncounted variant sessions the median is 9.2615 s against a 60-session native median of 10.4565 s (-11.33%), and 79 of 80 variant sessions beat the FASTEST of the 60 native sessions. The instability is itself part of the finding.

EXPLANATIONS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, with the number that rejected them. (1) 'The date+interval dialect cast penalises PostgreSQL' — REJECTED: removing it makes PostgreSQL 1.0040% SLOWER, inside its own 0.811% band; sign wrong, magnitude noise. (2) 'CUBRID wins because it has the better plan' — REJECTED: node-for-node identical on every cost-carrying stage with identical row counts; the sole node difference is 0.4907% and runs AGAINST CUBRID. (3) 'PostgreSQL cannot parallelise an uncorrelated scalar subquery' — REJECTED outright by the mpw12 control (4.484525 s, InitPlan launches 5). (4) 'IMP-020 explains CUBRID's CPU' — REJECTED for Q15: that band is 11.480 against 10.610 core-s, +8.2% NEAR PARITY, because Q15 projects 4 of 16 lineitem columns and PostgreSQL's own tts_buffer_heap_getsomeattrs costs 8.703 core-s; Q15 is NOT filed as an IMP-020 relation. (5) 'CUBRID's aggregation is the problem' — REJECTED, sign inverted: CUBRID's group-by band is 1.288 core-s CHEAPER. (6) 'CUBRID is stalling on memory' — REJECTED: IPC 1.99 against 1.84. (7) 'The 80.46% miss rate is purely a replacement-policy failure' — PARTIALLY REJECTED as stated: 1.214x storage density is a genuine co-cause and is recorded separately. (8) 'Q15's near-parity means CUBRID is competitive on this shape' — REJECTED as over-generalisation; see the mpw12 control.

WHAT REMAINS AFTER THE CONFIGURATION IS EQUALISED. Q15 becomes a 2.3291x PostgreSQL win and the explanation is no longer parallelism at all — it is F_cost: 331.11 against 170.33 ns of CPU per identical row, with 12.464 of the 18.358 core-s gap localised to the buffer+page-read path (+9.358) and predicate evaluation (+3.524).

Every cost-carrying node is identical: two sequential revenue0 expansions, each a filtered lineitem scan feeding a group-by over 100,000 supplier groups, then a single-row PK index lookup on supplier. It is NOT cosmetic — it changes the comparison TYPE, and the plans prove it: CUBRID filters date-vs-DATE (range date '01/01/1996' ge_lt date '04/01/1996'), PostgreSQL native filters date-vs-TIMESTAMP (l_shipdate < '1996-04-01 00:00:00'::timestamp without time zone). headline_finding: Q15's contract ratio is 0.979380x with CUBRID marginally FASTER — and the report's own headline is that this number is a property of the CONFIGURED WORKER BUDGET, not of the engines' capability. Q15 is the first query in the campaign that needs TWO CONCURRENT PARALLEL SUBTREES, because revenue0 is referenced twice (once as the join's input, once inside max(total_revenue)) and neither engine reuses the first expansion. SSOT s9 configures max_parallel_workers=100 for CUBRID against 5 for PostgreSQL, a non-parity s9 states explicitly ('not global-worker parity'). CUBRID runs BOTH expansions at 6 workers (5560 ms and 5528 ms). PostgreSQL runs one at 6 units (2340 ms) and the other at ONE unit (8817 ms) because the sibling Gather Merge already holds all 5 global slots when the lazily-evaluated InitPlan asks for workers, so it reports 'Workers Launched: 0'. One 2.38x win against one 1.59x loss nearly cancels, which is the whole reason Q15 lands near 1.0. Give PostgreSQL a GLOBAL pool of 12 with the per-gather cap unchanged at 5 and both subtrees launch 5: 4.484525 s, i.e. 2.3782x faster than its own contract number and 2.3291x faster than CUBRID.

Attached to verified PID sets: CUBRID's single multithreaded cub_server 1612732 (32 TIDs, all query workers inside that one process); PostgreSQL attached to the POSTMASTER 1433696 BEFORE the client connected so inherit-on-fork counts the leader and every statement's workers. Coverage validated against perf stat: ZERO [unknown] symbol lines and ZERO lost samples on both sides (CUBRID 190,340 samples / 800 flat lines; PostgreSQL 84,385 / 1,849). No all-CPU profile.

perf stat: CUBRID 463.53G cycles, 922.10G instructions, IPC 1.99, task-clock 168.865 core-s, 3.752 CPUs utilized. PostgreSQL 246.30G cycles, 452.82G instructions, IPC 1.84, 87.919 core-s, 1.954 CPUs utilized. Per logical session: 1,784 against 894 instructions per lineitem row read (1.996x), which independently reproduces F_cost 1.9439x. CUBRID's IPC is HIGHER — it is not stalling, it retires twice the instructions for the same row.

CUBRID top bands (% of profile -> absolute core-s per session, total 39.194): record/slot decode + MVCC header 16.86% -> 6.608 (or_mvcc_get_repid_and_flags 2.34, or_mvcc_get_header 1.90, spage_get_record_data 1.60, heap_next_1page 3.92, heap_scan_get_visible_version 2.13, ...); sarg/predicate evaluation 15.20% -> 5.957 (eval_pred 6.88, tp_value_compare_with_error 4.11, eval_value_rel_cmp 2.44, eval_data_filter 1.77); per-row DB_VALUE materialisation 12.43% -> 4.872 (heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues 8.97, pr_clear_value 1.18, fetch_val_list 1.53); PAGE READ kernel copy 11.67% -> 4.574 (rep_movs_alternative 9.76, call graph __libc_pread64 <- fileio_read <- pgbuf_claim_bcb_for_fix <- pgbuf_fix_release); BUFFER VICTIM SEARCH 10.19% -> 3.994 (pgbuf_get_victim_candidates_from_lru); buffer fix/unfix/latch+mutex 4.94% -> 1.936; parallel scan slot iteration 2.70% -> 1.058; sort/group-by merge 2.58% -> 1.011; numeric arithmetic 0.70% -> 0.274. Sum of these gaps +12.464 of the total measured +18.358 core-s.
ranking_rationale: IMP-007 + IMP-002 first: 9.358 core-s, 51% of the measured CPU gap, and the only band where CUBRID is an ORDER OF MAGNITUDE away rather than a factor of two. IMP-008 second: 3.524 core-s, 19%, and cheapest to reason about because the qual is a single date range on one column. IMP-015 third: worth >=11% of WALL and the only one of the five that moves F_units rather than F_cost, but ranked third because its status is a bound rather than a direct A/B and because the faster path is also the less stable one (5.68% trailing spread). IMP-013 fourth: real at 1.936 core-s but largely a consequence of the miss volume IMP-002/IMP-007 govern, so fixing those shrinks it automatically. source_contrast:
Every row is a concrete file:line on BOTH sides, with its s17 class.

1. GLOBAL PARALLEL-WORKER BUDGET WHEN A SECOND SUBTREE ASKS FOR WORKERS [same stage, lower measured cost — but CONFIGURED]. CUBRID src/query/parallel/px_worker_manager_global.cpp:57,77-78 sizes the pool from PRM_ID_MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS (=100 here) and :97-138 try_reserve_workers() grants a PARTIAL reservation ('reserve as many as possible, up to requested'). PostgreSQL src/backend/postmaster/bgworker.c:1103-1112 RegisterDynamicBackgroundWorker() returns false for every parallel worker once parallel_register_count - parallel_terminate_count >= max_parallel_workers (=5 here) and the requester silently proceeds with what it got. CUBRID's second 6-worker expansion draws from 94 free slots; PostgreSQL's second gather finds 0 of 5 and reports Workers Launched: 0. Classified with care: the CODE difference is real, but the MEASURED outcome on Q15 is produced by the campaign's configured values, which s9 declares deliberately non-parity — so it is filed as neither a PostgreSQL defect nor a CUBRID advantage.

2. WHEN THE UNCORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY IS EVALUATED [structural absence]. CUBRID src/query/query_executor.c — rewritten statement 2 is a separate SUBQUERY (uncorrelated) executed before the join consumes its outer input. PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/nodeSubplan.c:1094-1118 ExecSetParamPlan(), reached from ExecEvalParamExec() — an InitPlan is evaluated LAZILY at first reference to its PARAM_EXEC. CUBRID evaluates its second expansion while no other parallel subtree holds workers; PostgreSQL's lazy evaluation lands it INSIDE the sibling gather's lifetime.

3. PARALLELISM OF A SORT-BASED GROUP BY [structural absence]. CUBRID src/storage/external_sort.c:5229-5234 sort_check_parallelism(): 'if (px == NULL || px->hash_eligible) return 1;', with the flag set purely syntactically at src/parser/xasl_generation.c:16555-16571 (hint or aggregate-type tree walk, NO cost comparison). PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c + nodeGatherMerge.c — the partial aggregate runs inside every parallel worker and Gather Merge finalises; no flag disables the parallel path merely because hashing is possible. CUBRID's group-by runs serial (5,280 ms of 11,121 ms at 1 unit) whenever hash aggregation is merely ELIGIBLE.

4. SERVING A BUFFER MISS [same stage, lower measured cost]. CUBRID src/storage/page_buffer.c — pgbuf_claim_bcb_for_fix -> fileio_read -> __libc_pread64, a synchronous single-page pread on the query thread (4.574 core-s), plus pgbuf_get_victim_candidates_from_lru LRU victim search (3.994 core-s). PostgreSQL src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c — clock-sweep PinBuffer/StrategyGetBuffer with no per-page LRU list surgery (PinBuffer + LWLockAttemptLock = 0.338 core-s). 10.504 against 1.146 core-s for the same ZERO-device-read workload.

5. EVALUATING THE SCAN RANGE PREDICATE [same stage, lower measured cost]. CUBRID eval_pred -> eval_value_rel_cmp -> tp_value_compare_with_error, a generic DB_VALUE comparator with per-call domain resolution (5.957 core-s over 119,972,104 rows). PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/execExprInterp.c ExecInterpExpr — the qual compiled once into type-specialised ExprEvalSteps (2.434 core-s over the same rows). 2.45x on the identical predicate and rows.

6. DOUBLE EVALUATION OF THE VIEW [COMMON TO BOTH ENGINES]. CUBRID: two rewritten statements, each a full scan + group-by. PostgreSQL: InitPlan expr_1 plus the outer branch, each a full scan + aggregate. Neither engine reuses the first expansion, so this cancels out of the card entirely and is NOT filed as a CUBRID candidate — though it is the reason Q15 needs two parallel subtrees at once.

Claims of absence were searched, not assumed: hash_eligible was traced across src/parser/xasl_generation.c, src/query/query_executor.c, src/query/parallel/px_scan/, src/query/xasl.h, src/query/{xasl_to_stream,stream_to_xasl}.c and src/storage/external_sort.{c,h} with patterns hash_eligible, g_hash_eligible, sort_check_parallelism, SORT_GROUP_BY.

buffer_state_of_the_headline:
Q16 is the FIRST query in the campaign with ZERO PHYSICAL READS ON BOTH ENGINES, so none of its 3.031730x F_cost is I/O and none of the campaign's buffer-retention candidates (IMP-002 / IMP-007 / IMP-018) fires here.
PostgreSQL: pg_stat_database.blks_read 761,539,937 -> 761,539,937 across a four-statement block, delta 0; /proc/<postmaster>/io read_bytes delta 0; pg_statio heap+idx reads on Q16's relations delta 0; /proc/diskstats device read delta 0.000 MiB.
CUBRID: /proc/<cub_server>/io read_bytes delta 0 and rchar delta 14,912 B across the WHOLE four-statement block (3,728 B per statement -- three orders of magnitude below one 16 KiB page), write_bytes delta 4,096 B. The entire working set (part 380.5 MiB plus the partsupp covering index) is resident in the 8192 MB pool, and the 27,840 per-group temp list files never reach a write syscall.
NOTE THE DIRECTION: PostgreSQL reads MORE from the OS on Q16 (63.8 MB per statement of rchar) than CUBRID does, because its external-merge sort spills 12 MB per worker (Sort Method: external merge Disk: 12136kB x 5, temp read=7574 written=7594). The faster engine is the one doing more OS I/O; the difference is temp-sort traffic, not table I/O.
EVIDENCE-INTEGRITY: `cubrid statdump` remains UNUSABLE on this server, reconfirming the Q14 finding -- delta 0 on Num_data_page_fetches, Num_data_page_ioreads, Num_data_page_dirties and every other counter across a full block in -c mode while /proc recorded real (small) activity. Those snapshots are retained with an explicit invalid reason and EXCLUDED from every calculation.
carried_forward_gaps: F_cost 3.031730x is attributed by profile bands, not by a controlled A/B -- the same evidence class as Q12/Q13/Q14's F_cost. The bands are disjoint self-% partitions of a 0-unknown-symbol profile, but no switch isolates any single one.

IMP-023's sub-item (a) (presorted-input DISTINCT) is MEASURED to be worth -7.06% on Q16, so the candidate's recommended fix is (b)/(c), whose effect is bounded (0.750-1.041 s per statement) but not directly A/B-tested; no CUBRID switch exists to test it without a code change. Status stays 'measured', not 'validated'.

IMP-022's Q16 wall effect is exactly zero. Its magnitude is established (36.61x, pattern-independent, reproduced from source constants) but no query in Q01-Q16 has yet been measured to lose wall time to that specific branch.

The 5x uncorrelated-subquery materialisation (IMP-009) is quantified in CPU (~0.49 core-s, 5.2%) but its source line was NOT located in this session; the evidence is the trace counter pair (readrows 500,000 vs 100,000), not a code citation.

cubrid statdump remains unusable for per-statement buffer accounting on this server (Q14 finding, reconfirmed). CUBRID buffer evidence uses /proc/<pid>/io and /proc/diskstats, which are whole-process and cannot be split per plan node.

PostgreSQL's presorted-aggregate mis-costing (the F_plan anchor) is a real, measured PostgreSQL defect surfaced by this campaign's instrument. It is out of scope for the CUBRID improvement ledger and is recorded in the report only, deliberately.
causal_decomposition_narrative:
WHERE THE 1.689 s GOES. The interval series behind U and TWU, bucketed at the 1.5-active-unit threshold with actual sample timestamp deltas and divided by the four statements of each block:
  CUBRID native            serial-ish 1.041 s/statement (35.9% of the busy window), parallel 1.856 s at 4.498 units
  PostgreSQL nopresorted   serial-ish 0.291 s (26.2%),                                parallel 0.818 s at 3.422 units
  PostgreSQL native        serial-ish 0.147 s (12.2%),                                parallel 1.052 s at 3.390 units
Against the PLAN-CONTROLLED PostgreSQL leg -- same aggregation shape, same 27,840 per-group dedups, same 1,186,602 rows -- the serial phase is 3.5773x and the parallel phase 2.2689x. Both are slower; the serial one by 1.577x more. The serial differential alone, 1.041 - 0.291 = 0.750 s, is 44.4% OF Q16'S ENTIRE 1.689 s GAP. The CUBRID trace localises the same time independently as the gap between GROUPBY's total 1,471 ms and the 291-306 ms its three sort workers spend (~1,170 ms), and /proc shows 0 physical reads, so it is pure CPU in the post-sort finalize loop.

THE 36.61x SELECTIVITY ERROR, REPRODUCED FROM SOURCE CONSTANTS. Ten non-executing plan dumps against exact count(*) on both engines. SIX ANCHORED PATTERNS WHOSE TRUE SELECTIVITIES SPAN 0.833 TO 1.000 ALL RECEIVE THE BYTE-IDENTICAL ESTIMATE 0.0263974, including 'ZZZZZ%', a prefix no row has: not like 'MEDIUM POLISHED%' (true card 1,933,121), 'ZZZZZ%' (2,000,000), 'MEDIUM%' (1,666,123), 'M%' (1,666,123), 'MEDIUM POLISHED' with no wildcard at all (1,933,121), 'M' (1,933,121) -- all estimated at card 52,795. The estimate is PATTERN-INDEPENDENT, so it is not a data problem. Writing S = matched_mcv_freq + nonmcv_mass x total_non_mcv_sel divided by (1 - nullfrac) (histogram_cl.cpp:1545-1553), with the non-MCV mass factor 0.9737 and MCV mass 0.0263 read off the two patterns that match every value (LIKE '%' and LIKE '_%' both give 0.99990263 = 0.0263 + 0.9737 x 0.9999), every probe reconstructs exactly: 'MEDIUM POLISHED%' -> prefix skipped, remainder '%' -> 5.0 clamped to 1.0 -> upper clamp 0.9999 -> 0.9737 x 0.9999 = 0.97360263 -> NOT LIKE 0.02639737 (printed 0.0263974); 'MEDIUM POLISHED' -> no wildcard -> return 1.0 at :1334-1337 -> same; 'MEDIUM POLISHED_' -> remainder '_' -> ANY_CHAR_SEL 0.90 -> 0.876330 -> NOT LIKE 0.123670 (printed 0.12367); '%M' -> '%'->1.0 then FIXED_CHAR_SEL 0.20 -> 0.194740 -> NOT LIKE 0.805260 (printed 0.80526); '%MEDIUM POLISHED%' -> 0.20^15 x 5 = 1.6384e-10 -> lower clamp 0.0001 -> 9.737e-05 (printed 0.999903). Five exact reconstructions to 7 significant digits. AND IT COST Q16 NOTHING: the 39.24x conjunct error did not change the plan.

WHAT THE RESIDUAL IS MADE OF. After F_plan is anchored away, F_cpu 3.031730x on F_work exactly 1.000000x is the whole story, and the bands partition it. Ranked by absolute CUBRID core-seconds above PostgreSQL, of a 5.8217 core-s CPU differential: D predicate evaluation +1.3206 (22.7%), E row materialisation +1.0058 (17.3%), C LIKE matcher +0.7938 (13.6%), A sort/group-by/DISTINCT +0.5630 (9.7%), B anti-join membership +0.4138 (7.1%), F index scan +0.3158 (5.4%), rest +1.4089 (24.2%). BAND A BEING ONLY 9.7% OF THE CPU DIFFERENTIAL WHILE OWNING 44.4% OF THE WALL DIFFERENTIAL IS NOT A CONTRADICTION -- IT IS THE POINT: band A's excess is concentrated in the phase that runs at ~1 active unit, so each of its core-seconds buys 1 second of wall, while bands D/E/C are spread across the 4.5-unit parallel phase where each core-second buys ~0.22 s. This is why IMP-023 is ranked first despite not owning the largest CPU band.

EXPLANATIONS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, WITH THE NUMBER THAT REJECTED THEM:
1. 'CUBRID's count(DISTINCT) plan shape is wrong.' REJECTED by the other engine's own switch: forced into CUBRID's shape PostgreSQL is 1.075998x FASTER (1.112363 vs 1.196902 s). F_plan 0.929368x. The shape is fine; the implementation of the shape is not.
2. 'CUBRID's parallelism is worse.' REJECTED by F_units 0.855774x -- CUBRID runs at MORE active units (3.28929 vs 2.81489 controlled, 3.06804 native) with a nearly identical peak (5.2129 vs 5.1941) -- and by CUBRID's own NO_PARALLEL_SCAN A/B: 2.6646x speedup for a 17.60% CPU surcharge, 81.0% efficiency against U.
3. 'The group-by sort refuses to parallelise' (IMP-015). REJECTED by the trace: GROUPBY ... (parallel workers: 3) in BOTH the native and the NO_PARALLEL_SCAN run. sort_check_parallelism() admitted it. Q16's serial phase is the POST-SORT loop, a different code path.
4. 'Hash aggregation was abandoned' (IMP-016/IMP-017). REJECTED by both engines agreeing: CUBRID's plan is hash: false, sort: true, and PostgreSQL independently costs GroupAggregate below HashAggregate. Neither engine chose hashing, so neither abandoned it.
5. 'CUBRID is short of buffer memory / re-reading pages' (IMP-002/IMP-007/IMP-018). REJECTED by 0 physical reads: /proc/<cub_server>/io moves 14,912 B of rchar, 0 read_bytes and 4,096 B write_bytes across a whole four-statement block.
6. 'The cardinality error picked the wrong plan.' REJECTED by the plan text: despite a 39.24x under-estimate on the part conjunct, CUBRID's skeleton is node-for-node the one PostgreSQL chose. Registered as IMP-022 with ZERO Q16 wall time attributed.
7. 'The 5x subquery re-execution is the cost.' BOUNDED and rejected as a WALL explanation: 400,000 redundant supplier rows at the serial run's 123 ms per 100,000 rows is ~0.49 core-s of 9.4929 (5.2% of CPU), and the five copies run CONCURRENTLY, so the wall effect is near zero. Recorded against IMP-009 as a CPU-efficiency item, explicitly not double-counted against IMP-023's serial band.
8. 'PostgreSQL wins because it does less I/O.' REJECTED by direction: PostgreSQL reads MORE from the OS (63.8 MB/statement of rchar vs CUBRID's 3,728 B) because its external-merge sort spills. Both take zero DEVICE reads.

cubrid_trace_finding:
SET TRACE ON + SHOW TRACE. Total SELECT time 3069 ms.
  SCAN part      heap time 1581, parallel workers: 5, readrows 399448..401913 (= 2,000,000)
    SCAN index partsupp.pk_partsupp_ps_partkey_ps_suppkey  btree time 1188,
         readkeys 1484120, filteredkeys 1186602, rows 1186602, covered: true, ioread 0
  GROUPBY  time 1471, hash: false, sort: true, rows 27840,
           parallel workers: 3, time 291..306, page 6846..7174, ioread 0
  ORDERBY  time 17
  SUBQUERY (uncorrelated): SCAN supplier readrows 500000, rows 280

THREE READINGS, each cross-checked against ground truth and against the NO_PARALLEL_SCAN trace of the same query:
1. readkeys 1,484,120 decomposes EXACTLY as 1,187,296 matched partsupp rows + 296,824 index searches. So CUBRID performs exactly 296,824 searches -- identical to PostgreSQL's 'Index Searches: 296824' -- and filteredkeys 1,186,602 is exactly the ground-truth ps_after_antijoin. The part sargs ARE applied before the probe, despite the parallel node reporting rows == readrows (a per-worker trace-counter artifact; the serial run correctly reports rows: 296824).
2. GROUPBY time 1471 against parallel workers: 3, time 291..306. Only ~300 ms of the 1,471 ms group-by is inside the sort workers. THE REMAINING ~1,170 ms IS THE POST-SORT SCAN/FINALIZE LOOP, and it matches the independently measured 1.041 s sub-1.5-active-unit phase. Two instruments, same phase.
3. SCAN supplier readrows 500000 on a 100,000-row table: the uncorrelated NOT IN subquery is materialised ONCE PER PARALLEL SCAN WORKER -- exactly 5x -- which the NO_PARALLEL_SCAN trace confirms by reporting readrows 100000, rows 56. 400,000 redundant rows and 400,000 redundant leading-wildcard LIKE evaluations per statement.
dedup_statement:
TWO NEW IDS WERE ALLOCATED, and the search that justified them is recorded. The Git ledger was synced (git fetch/pull --ff-only; HEAD = origin/main = 1c9c618) and searched by title, CUBRID source location, PostgreSQL source location and root cause against all 21 existing candidates before either allocation.
(a) IMP-003 already owns histogram_cl.cpp:1427 histogram_get_like_selectivity() and query_planner.c:10068 qo_like_selectivity(). Its defect is the NON-MCV BUCKET-BOUNDARY arm (:1487-1501) on a LEADING-WILDCARD pattern producing an UNDER-estimate. Q16's s_comment predicate is exactly that case and was added to IMP-003 as evidence, NOT as a new ID. Q16's OTHER LIKE defect is a different code line in a different arm (:1300-1337 pattern_heuristic_selectivity, the fixed-prefix skip), fires only on an ANCHORED pattern, only through the PT_NOT_LIKE branch at query_planner.c:9939-9943, and errs in the OPPOSITE direction. Folding it into IMP-003 would hide a distinct, independently fixable line, so it is IMP-022 with an explicit sibling relation.
(b) IMP-006 owns list-file materialisation of INTERMEDIATE JOIN RESULTS (qexec_end_one_iteration / qfile_generate_tuple_into_list). IMP-023 is a different list file created by different code for a different reason: one temp file PER GROUP, created by qdata_process_distinct_or_sort(), fed by qdata_evaluate_aggregate_list() and consumed by qdata_finalize_aggregate_list(). Related, not the same root cause; a containment note was added to IMP-006.
(c) IMP-015 (sort_check_parallelism refuses parallelism for SORT_GROUP_BY) does NOT fire on Q16 -- the trace shows the group-by sort DID parallelise at 3 workers -- and a containment note recording that was added.
(d) IMP-016/IMP-017 (hash aggregation abandoned / mis-parameterised) do not fire: the plan is hash: false, sort: true BY CHOICE on both engines.
Q16 evidence and Q relations were added to IMP-003, IMP-004, IMP-008, IMP-009 and IMP-020. next_id advanced IMP-022 -> IMP-024.

f_plan_anchor:
PostgreSQL exposes the exact decision as a GUC, which is what makes Q16's F_plan a direct same-engine A/B instead of an UNMEASURED. With enable_presorted_aggregate=off, adjust_group_pathkeys_for_groupagg() returns immediately (planner.c:3516-3517), group_pathkeys is not extended with the DISTINCT aggregate's pathkey, aggref->aggpresorted stays false, and nodeAgg.c:4268 sets pertrans->aggsortrequired = true -- a per-group tuplesort. That is CUBRID's shape.

The controlled plan differs from the native plan in EXACTLY ONE LINE:
  native:      Sort Key: part.p_brand, part.p_type, part.p_size, partsupp.ps_suppkey
  nopresorted: Sort Key: part.p_brand, part.p_type, part.p_size
Every other node AND every printed cost is byte-identical -- Parallel Hash Anti Join (cost=2991.80..151550.34 rows=299086), Gather Merge (cost=187932.07..331176.12 rows=1196346), GroupAggregate (cost=187932.07..344681.44 rows=154186), Sort (cost=362713.89..363099.36). So the A/B isolates the DISTINCT-aggregate strategy and nothing else.

Measured: native 1.196902 s, controlled 1.112363 s. F_plan = 0.929368x. Every sub-measurement moves in the predicted direction: worker sort spill 12,136 -> 12,040 kB (-0.8%), worker sort completes 714.856 -> 607.108 ms (-15.1%), parallel-phase time per statement 1.052 -> 0.818 s (-22.2%), serial-ish time per statement 0.147 -> 0.291 s (+98.0%), CPU 3.6721 -> 3.1312 core-s (-14.7%). The narrower sort saves more than the per-group tuplesort costs, and the net is 7.06% in CUBRID's shape's favour.

This is also a genuine finding about POSTGRESQL, recorded because the campaign measures both engines with the same instrument: on Q16 PostgreSQL's own presorted-aggregate optimization is a NET LOSS of 7.06%, because adjust_group_pathkeys_for_groupagg() extends the sort key without costing the extra sort column against the per-group tuplesort it avoids. It is not an improvement candidate for this campaign (whose subject is CUBRID) but it is the reason F_plan is below 1.0, so it is stated explicitly rather than folded into a residual.

headline_finding: Q16 is the first query in this campaign where TWO of the three causal factors are BELOW 1.0, and both of them refute the obvious story. R_wall is 2.411225x (PostgreSQL faster), but F_plan is 0.929368x -- CUBRID's plan shape is the BETTER one -- and F_units is 0.855774x -- CUBRID runs at MORE active units. The entire gap is F_cost 3.031730x on F_work EXACTLY 1.000000x: both engines scan the same 2,000,000 part rows, perform the same 296,824 index searches into partsupp, carry the same 1,186,602 rows into grouping and emit the same 27,840 groups, and both take ZERO physical reads. buffer_state_of_the_headline:
CUBRID: ZERO physical reads. Trace reports ioread: 0 at the SELECT level and every scan node (q17-trace-cubrid.out); telemetry recorded process read_bytes=0 and device sectors_read=0 on every data device; a statdump delta taken with adequate flush latency around ONE execution shows 161,531 page fetches against +1 Num_data_page_ioreads. Statdump deltas taken immediately around the 0.59 s block read as exactly zero on all three blocks -- a flush-latency artifact of sampling a sub-second window (the Q14/Q16 finding, reconfirmed), not a zero-fetch claim, so the WARM proof rests on trace, procfs and device evidence rather than those block gauges.
PostgreSQL native: CANNOT reach zero physical reads, by construction. heap_blks_read deltas 937,800 / 887,112 / 836,424 per 4-statement block (~234k/222k/209k per statement, ~1.8 GB); EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirms read=196866 for a single statement. lineitem occupies 1,125,128 blocks against shared_buffers of 1,048,576 blocks, so the plan PostgreSQL chose provably does not fit the configured-equal 8192 MB budget -- yet the engine is at steady state (level converged, within-block spread 0.16%), so this is WARM in the steady-state sense the contract requires, with residual reads recorded rather than hidden.
PostgreSQL controlled (nlj): ZERO physical reads. heap_blks_read delta 0 and an identical heap_blks_hit delta of 8,026,344 in all three blocks; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Buffers: shared hit=2198652 with no read=. The plan PostgreSQL REJECTED is fully resident.
The controlled cross-engine pair used for F_units and F_cpu is therefore a zero-physical-read pair on BOTH sides, removing I/O residency as a confound from those two factors and confining it entirely to F_plan.
carried_forward_gaps: F_cost's 1.366905x is attributed by profile bands (attribute-materialisation and predicate-evaluation ratios), not by a single controlled A/B that isolates it from F_work; the same evidence class as several earlier queries' F_cost.

IMP-012's Q17 evidence is a projection (upper bound), not a direct A/B: PRM_ID_PARALLELISM lacks PRM_USER_CHANGE, confirmed by the silently-accepted-but-ineffective 'parallelism=1' attempt, so no in-session degree A/B could be run on this query or any other in the campaign without a code change.

IMP-019's Q17 relation has an explicitly zero measured wall effect; the 0.1 placeholder selectivity is established as pattern-independent for this arm but no query yet measured has lost wall time to it.

IMP-005's Q17 evidence newly shows the traced subquery-cache 'size' counter is also inflated by the same (k-1) parallel-merge defect, making it unusable for operator capacity planning; no CUBRID-side fix has been scoped for the size counter specifically, only the count counters.

The uncorrelated hypothesis about a subquery-cache disable cliff was bounded up to 16,030 keys (7.8x Q17's actual 2,044) without triggering, but the true disable threshold at subquery_cache.c:378-383 was not identified from source in this session -- only that the traced 'size' is not the compared quantity.

PostgreSQL's own weaknesses surfaced by Q17 (no correlated-SubPlan memo, unparallelisable join with a correlated SubPlan in its qual) are recorded only in reports/Q17/report.md sections 7-8, deliberately out of scope for the CUBRID-only improvement ledger; no cross-campaign tracking mechanism exists yet for PostgreSQL-side findings across queries.
causal_decomposition_narrative:
F_plan 8.9166x [CUBRID-faster form] -- PostgreSQL's plan choice, anchored by a same-engine A/B. Forcing enable_hashjoin=off moves PostgreSQL from 8.754980 s to 0.981877 s; the controlled plan is structurally CUBRID's (seq-scan filtered part, index-probe lineitem). Three measured consequences folded into this factor, none double-counted elsewhere: lineitem rows scanned 59,986,052 vs 61,385 (977x); physical reads 196,866/statement vs 0; IPC 1.44 vs 2.38. PostgreSQL's own cost model ranks the two plans backwards by 3.34x, pinned to how the join-qual SubPlan is charged -- 61,385 executions at ~112.98 each in the nested loop, ~0.14 each in the hash join, for work both actual plans confirm is identical (loops=61385 in both).

F_units 4.9209x -- CUBRID parallelises, PostgreSQL cannot. U_C 4.92437 vs U_Pc 1.00071, cross-checked by perf stat CPUs-utilized (4.892/0.972) and TWU (4.6063/1.0081). PostgreSQL's controlled plan is entirely serial -- serial tail equals its whole busy window, 4.027 s of 4.027 s -- because the correlated SubPlan is parallel-restricted so the joinrel has no partial path, and the outer part scan cannot parallelise under a nested loop whose inner is parameterised. CUBRID runs the same part scan at 5 workers.

F_cpu 1.3667x = F_work 1.8681x fewer x F_cost 1.3669x more per tuple. F_work is almost entirely the subquery memo: part heap band 2,000,000 rows on both sides (exact parity, no index on (p_brand,p_container) on either engine); outer lineitem index band 61,385 on both sides; the SUBQUERY band is 61,385 rows on CUBRID against 1,903,163 on PostgreSQL -- 31.0x -- because CUBRID executes the subquery 2,044 times and PostgreSQL 61,385 times, and 2,044 is exactly the number of distinct qualifying p_partkey values (ground truth), the strongest possible confirmation the memo key is the correlation value and hits on every repeat. F_cost is CUBRID's per-row overhead on a plan-shape-controlled denominator: 338.69 ns vs 247.78 ns per executor tuple read, both sides warm with zero physical reads; attributed by profile to attribute materialisation/value lifecycle (2.84x/tuple) and predicate evaluation (1.72x/part row), partially offset by CUBRID's 5.8x LOWER buffer-management cost.

DIRECT A/B ON THE MEMO ITSELF. max_subquery_cache_size carries PRM_USER_CHANGE, so same engine/plan/warm-state: 2 MB (default) -> 0.161 s wall, 31 ms subquery band, SUBQUERY_CACHE hit 118,682/miss 4,088 enabled; 0 (cache off) -> 0.784 s wall, 645 ms subquery band, cache absent; 16 MB -> 0.161 s (unchanged; the default is not binding). The memo is worth 4.87x on CUBRID's Q17 (0.784 -> 0.161 s), the subquery band alone moves 20.8x (645 -> 31 ms). Even with the memo DISABLED, CUBRID (0.784 s) still beats PostgreSQL's controlled plan (0.982 s) and native plan (8.755 s) -- the memo explains most of F_work but none of F_plan or F_units.

EXPLANATIONS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, with the number that rejected each:
1. 'CUBRID's subquery cache is one entry from the disable cliff' (trace size 1,980,048 against a 2 MB budget = 94.4% full at 2,044 keys). REJECTED: a probe with 4,051 distinct keys still reported status=enabled; a probe with 16,030 distinct keys (7.8x Q17's) also retained every key (miss 32,060 = 2x16,030) status=enabled; both reported a traced size LARGER than the 2 MB budget they ran under, and an explicit 1,500,000-byte budget run reported size 1,539,408 and stayed enabled. The traced size is not the quantity compared at the cliff check; no candidate raised.
2. 'CUBRID takes zero page fetches, served from a higher-level cache.' REJECTED: statdump deltas around the 0.59 s block read exactly 0, but a delta around a single execution with adequate flush latency shows +161,531 fetches and +1 ioread -- a statistics-flush-latency artifact of sampling a sub-second window, not a fetch-free scan.
3. 'PostgreSQL's disadvantage is buffer-management cost, IMP-013 reversed.' REJECTED as the primary cause: PostgreSQL's buffer band is indeed 5.8x CUBRID's (0.37327 vs 0.06413 core-s), but that 0.309 core-s sits inside a controlled pair whose total CPU gap is only 0.264 core-s in CUBRID's favour, and it explains none of the 8.9x F_plan; recorded in section 6 as a counter-example, not support.
4. 'The sel 0.1 placeholder for l_quantity < (subquery) misleads CUBRID's optimizer.' REJECTED: CUBRID's join-output estimate is 5,975 against a true 5,526 (8.1% error) and it selected the optimal plan; the placeholder is real but costs nothing on Q17.
5. 'CUBRID wins because PostgreSQL's working set does not fit shared_buffers.' REJECTED as a SEPARABLE factor: the 196,866 physical reads/statement are real but occur only in the native plan; the controlled plan takes zero. The effect is inside F_plan and is not an independent buffer-budget finding -- the configured-equal 8192 MB budget is adequate for the plan PostgreSQL declined to use.

Effects are not summed: F_plan, F_units and F_cpu multiply; F_work/F_cost decompose F_cpu alone; the buffer band and the physical reads are named once each, in the factor that owns them.

f_plan_anchor:
F_plan is NUMERIC, anchored on a same-engine PostgreSQL native/controlled A/B: enable_hashjoin=off via PGOPTIONS, query text untouched. Native 8.754980 s -> controlled 0.981877 s = F_plan 0.112151x (8.9166x in CUBRID-faster form). The controlled plan is structurally CUBRID's own shape (seq-scan filtered part, index-probe lineitem on idx_fk_lineitem_partsupp), so F_units and F_cpu are then computed on the remaining controlled cross-engine pair (CUBRID native vs PostgreSQL-nlj) rather than against the native PostgreSQL plan -- native and controlled denominators are never mixed.

Mechanism behind the anchor: PostgreSQL's planner charges the correlated SubPlan in the join qual per-inner-candidate-row under the nested loop (Index Scan cost=0.44..3161.12, i.e. 27 candidate rows x 112.98) but only a fraction of that under the hash join's total of 1,933,196 (~8,515 cost units remain after the 1,725,001 outer seq scan + 49,686 hash build + 149,968 hash probe) -- far less than the same 61,385 evaluations would cost at 112.98 each. Both actual plans confirm loops=61385 for the SubPlan, so the two estimates disagree about IDENTICAL work; the cost model ranks the plans backwards by 3.34x (6,466,108 vs 1,933,196) while the controlled plan measures 8.92x faster.

Second mechanism, on why F_units is separately low for PostgreSQL rather than folded into F_plan: the correlated SubPlan is parallel-restricted at src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c:931-950 (max_parallel_hazard_walker rejects a SubPlan whose parallel_safe is false) and :960-973 (the subquery's own plan is parallel-restricted because the correlated p_partkey reference is a PARAM_EXEC Param not in safe_param_ids). The joinrel therefore never acquires a partial path, confirmed by forcing parallel costs to 0 (q17-plan-est-pg-parallel_forced.out) and still seeing Gather placed below the Hash Join. CUBRID has no such restriction and parallelises the driving part scan at 5 workers with the correlated subquery evaluated inside the scan.

headline_finding: Q17 is CUBRID's largest win in the campaign so far: median wall ratio T_C/T_P 0.016676x, i.e. PostgreSQL is 59.9656x SLOWER (CUBRID 0.146000 s vs PostgreSQL 8.754980 s). Unlike most of this campaign's queries, ALL THREE causal factors favour CUBRID and the plan itself is the dominant one: F_plan 0.112151x (PG's own cost model ranks the two candidate plans backwards by 3.34x and picks the 8.92x slower one), F_units 0.203216x (CUBRID parallelises the driving scan at ~5 units, PostgreSQL's plan cannot parallelise past its leader because the join's correlated SubPlan is parallel-restricted), and F_cpu 0.731709x = F_work 0.535303x x F_cost 1.366905x (CUBRID reads 1.8681x fewer executor tuples because it memoises the correlated subquery -- 2,044 executions vs PostgreSQL's 61,385 -- but costs 1.3669x more CPU per tuple read once the plan is controlled away). The single largest engineering finding is a POSTGRESQL weakness, not a CUBRID one: no memo for a correlated SubPlan (nodeSubplan.c:198-241) against CUBRID's sq_get/sq_put (fetch.c:4086-4111), plus an unparallelisable join whenever the join qual contains that SubPlan (clauses.c:931-950, :960-973).

plan_comparison_summary:
STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT plans, so F_plan is not 1.0 and is not assumed away. CUBRID drives from the filtered part side with an index nested loop into lineitem (idx-join, outer sscan part sargs container+brand cost 29353 card 1992, inner iscan lineitem index fk_lineitem_partsupp cost 57848 card 5975), evaluating the correlated subquery {p_partkey} <- node[1] once per outer candidate but MEMOISED on the correlation key. PostgreSQL natively drives from lineitem: Hash Join (cost=49711.16..1933195.71 rows=18496) with a Seq Scan on all 59,986,052 lineitem rows probing a 2,044-row part-derived hash table, and a Join Filter carrying the correlated SubPlan (Aggregate cost=112.98..112.99 -> Index Scan using idx_fk_lineitem_partsupp cost=0.44..112.91 rows=27).

Comparison table (native CUBRID / native PostgreSQL / controlled PostgreSQL-nlj): join method index-NL-part-outer / hash-join-lineitem-outer / index-NL-part-outer; lineitem rows touched for the join 61,385 (index) / 59,986,052 (seq) / 61,385 (index); part rows scanned 2,000,000 parallel-5-workers / 2,000,000 parallel-4-workers / 2,000,000 serial; correlated subquery invocations 61,385 on all three; correlated subquery EXECUTIONS 2,044 / 61,385 / 61,385; buffer accesses fetch 161,531/exec / 3,256,207 (196,866 physical) / 2,198,652 (0 physical); active units 4.92 / 1.09 / 1.00; estimated cost 57,848 / 1,933,196 / 6,466,108.

Two planner facts constitute the whole of F_plan: (1) PostgreSQL costs the winning nested loop at 6,466,108, 3.34x its own hash-join estimate of 1,933,196, yet the nested loop measures 8.92x FASTER -- the cost model mis-charges the correlated SubPlan in the join qual (per-inner-candidate-row in the NL vs a fraction of that in the hash join), even though both actual plans execute it exactly 61,385 times (loops=61385 in both). (2) The join can never be parallelised: with parallel_setup_cost=0, parallel_tuple_cost=0 and min_parallel_table_scan_size=0, PostgreSQL still places Gather BELOW the Hash Join, so the join and all 61,385 SubPlan executions stay in the leader -- U_P is 1.09, not ~6, because only the part scan is parallel.

source_contrast:
Six rows, concrete file:line on BOTH sides, searched not assumed for absence claims (searched nodeSubplan.c, nodeMemoize.c, subselect.c for useHashTable, hashtable, ExecHashSubPlan, Memoize, chgParam, ExecReScan; PostgreSQL's Memoize exists but is a nested-loop INNER-PATH cache keyed on join parameters (pathnode.c create_memoize_path, planned only in joinpath.c), not a SubPlan-expression cache, and no Memoize node appears in either Q17 plan).

1. Correlated scalar-subquery re-execution [structural absence]. CUBRID src/query/fetch.c:4086-4111 fetch_peek_dbval() case TYPE_CONSTANT: on an XASL_USES_SQ_CACHE subquery, sq_get() is tried first (subquery_cache.c:400-430); only on a miss does it execute and sq_put() (subquery_cache.c:290-393). PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/nodeSubplan.c:198-241 ExecScanSubPlan() unconditionally adds every parParam to chgParam and calls ExecReScan() -- full re-execution every time; useHashTable is set only for an UNCORRELATED ANY sublink (subselect.c:527-531), and Q17's is a correlated EXPR_SUBLINK so that path is unreachable (subselect.c's own comment: 'not interesting for parameter change signaling since we always re-evaluate the subplan'). Result: CUBRID executes the subquery 2,044 times for 61,385 invocations (96.7% hit rate); PostgreSQL executes it 61,385 times in BOTH of its plans (loops=61385 in both actual-plan captures) -- 30.03x fewer executions, exactly the 30 lineitem rows per matching part measured independently.

2. Parallelisation of a join whose qual contains a correlated subquery [structural absence]. CUBRID parallelises the driving part scan at 5 workers with the correlated subquery evaluated inside the scan (trace: parallel workers: 5, gather: buildvalue), reaching U_C 4.92. PostgreSQL src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c:931-950 max_parallel_hazard_walker rejects a SubPlan whose parallel_safe is false; parallel_safe is copied from the subquery's own plan (subselect.c:351), itself restricted because the correlated p_partkey reference is a PARAM_EXEC Param not in safe_param_ids (clauses.c:960-973). Measured, not inferred: forcing parallel_setup_cost=0, parallel_tuple_cost=0, min_parallel_table_scan_size=0 still places Gather BELOW the Hash Join, leaving the join and all 61,385 SubPlan executions in the leader; U_P 1.09, U_Pc 1.00 against CUBRID's 4.92.

3. Per-row materialisation of scan output [same stage, lower measured cost]. CUBRID src/storage/heap_file.c heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues() -- 15.18% of profile, reached from eval_data_filter once per part row; with mr_readval_char_internal 5.43%, db_value_domain_init 2.28%, pr_clear_value 3.07% the band is 27.51% -> 0.19779 core-s, 93.2 ns per tuple read. PostgreSQL src/backend/executor/execTuples.c tts_buffer_heap_getsomeattrs() -> slot_deform_heap_tuple() -- 12.19% -> 0.13019 core-s, 32.8 ns per tuple read; deforms into a flat Datum/isnull array via cached offsets, no per-value type object or teardown. 2.84x more CPU per tuple on the same plan shape, both sides zero physical reads.

4. Scan-level predicate evaluation [same stage, lower measured cost]. CUBRID eval_pred/eval_value_rel_cmp (query_evaluator.c) -> tp_value_compare_with_error (object_domain.c) -> mr_cmpval_char -> lang_fastcmp_byte -- 19.59% -> 0.14084 core-s, 70.4 ns per part row for the two bpchar equality sargs. PostgreSQL ExecInterpExpr (execExprInterp.c), qual compiled once into type-specialised steps calling bpchareq (varchar.c) directly -- 8.35% -> 0.08205 core-s, 41.0 ns per row. 1.72x more CPU for the identical two predicates over the identical 2,000,000 rows.

5. Buffer pin/unpin accounting [same stage, lower cost -- CUBRID favoured]. CUBRID pgbuf_fix_release 5.93% + pgbuf_unfix 1.31% + mutex band 1.30% = 8.92% -> 0.06413 core-s. PostgreSQL PinBuffer+StartReadBuffer+GetPrivateRefCountEntrySlow+LWLockRelease+UnpinBufferNoOwner+LWLockAttemptLock+LockBufferInternal+BufferLockUnlock+ResourceOwnerForget+hash_search_with_hash_value+hash_bytes+others = 37.99% -> 0.37327 core-s. PostgreSQL spends 5.8x more here, driven by 2,198,652 buffer accesses against CUBRID's memoised access pattern; counter-example to IMP-013 on this query.

6. Selectivity of attribute < (correlated subquery) [common to both engines]. CUBRID src/optimizer/query_planner.c:10498-10625 qo_comp_selectivity(): a subquery RHS falls to 'default: break' at :10558-10559, returning DEFAULT_COMP_SELECTIVITY 0.1 (query_planner.h:118), visible as term[0] ... (sel 0.1). PostgreSQL clausesel.c/selfuncs.c reach the same absence of statistics for a SubPlan result and fall back to DEFAULT_INEQ_SEL 0.3333 (selfuncs.h), giving rows=18496 against a true 5,526. Both engines guess and NEITHER side's guess changes the outcome: CUBRID chose the optimal plan regardless (estimate 5,975 vs true 5,526, only 8.1% error), and PostgreSQL's plan error is caused by the join-qual SubPlan costing in item 1/2, not by this selectivity.

This is a query CUBRID WINS, but the report's central claim is that the win is entirely a PostgreSQL plan-choice defect, not a CUBRID execution advantage: measured against PostgreSQL's own better plan (enable_indexscan=off, 30.681412s), CUBRID is 1.140993x worse on CPU and 1.069863x worse on active units. PostgreSQL's native optimizer places the IN-subquery GroupAggregate on the inner side of a Merge Join inside the parallel region, so all 6 parallel units independently re-scan the entire 59,986,052-row lineitem index (loops=6, 359,910,228 total fetches for work that logically needs 59,986,052). Two independent same-engine controls confirm this from opposite directions: enable_indexscan=off (30.681412s, 1.362x faster than native) and max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0 (24.282188s, 1.7209x faster than native).

plan_comparison_summary:
CUBRID (estimated, OPTIMIZATION LEVEL 514): rewrites o_orderkey IN (...) into a materialised derived table av1861, driven from that table via idx-join into orders/customer/lineitem by PK/FK -- the expensive subquery is evaluated exactly ONCE. CUBRID's own cardinality estimate for av1861 (14,929,885 vs a true 624, wrong by ~4 orders of magnitude) costs nothing because the resulting plan (drive from subquery, probe by unique key) is what a correct estimate would also produce. Subquery: temp(distinct) over temp(group by) over sscan lineitem, cost 1,308,583.

PostgreSQL (actual EXPLAIN ANALYZE): Limit -> Sort (top-N heapsort) -> Finalize GroupAggregate -> Gather Merge (5 workers) -> Partial GroupAggregate -> Sort -> Nested Loop -> Parallel Hash Join -> Merge Join (inner: GroupAggregate over Index Scan idx_fk_lineitem_orders rows=59985038.00 loops=6) -> Parallel Hash <- Parallel Seq Scan customer; outer Index Scan idx_fk_lineitem_orders rows=7 loops=624. The single most important line: the subquery's GroupAggregate sits on the INNER side of a Merge Join inside the parallel region, so it is NOT partitioned -- leader + 5 workers each independently scan the whole 59,986,052-row index and each discards the same 14,999,125 groups (per-worker rows: 59,979,968 / 59,986,052 x4 / leader 59,986,052). Total subquery lineitem fetches: 359,910,228, six times the logical requirement.

F_plan anchor (PostgreSQL native -> enable_indexscan=off): the subquery access path becomes Parallel Seq Scan, which the parallel machinery DOES partition -- Partial HashAggregate rows=2500295.50 loops=6 over Parallel Seq Scan lineitem_1 rows=9997675.33 loops=6 (9,997,675.33 x 6 = 59,986,052 exactly, table scanned exactly once in total, matching CUBRID's own parallel sscan readrows 9,938,887..10,011,920/worker). Measured 30.681412s against native 41.787122s, block CPU 350.46 core-s against 970.36 -- a 2.77x CPU reduction from deleting redundant work. Independent confirmation from the opposite direction: max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0 (native index-scan plan, but replication impossible with 1 unit) gives 24.282188s, 1.7209x faster than native -- two different switches, two different plan shapes, same conclusion.

Plan-comparison table: subquery evaluated once (CUBRID, materialised av1861) vs 6x once-per-unit (PostgreSQL native); subquery input access partitioned sscan (CUBRID, 6 workers x ~10M rows) vs replicated Index Scan (PostgreSQL native, 6 x 59.99M rows); subquery aggregation partial-hash-then-sort-spilling-422,017-pages (CUBRID) vs streaming GroupAggregate no-sort-no-spill (PostgreSQL); semijoin dedup extra temp(distinct) node (CUBRID, redundant) vs reduce_unique_semijoins proving uniqueness, Inner Unique:true (PostgreSQL); outer lineitem access iscan fk_lineitem_orders 4,368 rows (CUBRID) vs Index Scan 624 searches x 7 rows (PostgreSQL); parallelism actually achieved scan-phase-~6-units-groupby-phase-1-unit (CUBRID) vs ~5.67 units throughout (PostgreSQL). Each engine gets one thing right the other gets wrong: CUBRID evaluates the subquery once but aggregates it serially with a 6.4 GiB spill; PostgreSQL aggregates without sort/spill but pays for it six times over.
